entries.title: SQL Server on Azure Local is now generally available
entries.summary: With SQL Server on Azure Local, customers can modernize where their data resides while maintaining control over infrastructure, connectivity, and data placement. The post SQL Server on Azure Local is now generally available appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
Some of the world’s most critical databases run in places where cloud connectivity cannot be assumed. A remote industrial site, for example, may need production systems to continue operating when external connectivity is unavailable. A regulated organization may need sensitive data and processing to remain within sovereign boundaries.

Today, SQL Server on Azure Local is generally available for connected and disconnected operations. With this release, customers can modernize where their data resides while maintaining control over infrastructure, connectivity, and data placement. They can bring AI closer to their data with Foundry Local on Azure Local, currently in preview, and use eligible existing SQL Server licensing investments.

Run SQL Server where your data needs to stay

SQL Server has a long history of supporting mission-critical workloads on customer infrastructure. Azure Local builds on that flexibility by bringing Azure infrastructure to customer-owned environments, giving organizations a consistent platform for running SQL Server across datacenters and edge locations.

Customers can choose the deployment model that fits each environment:

  • Connected environments: Run SQL Server locally on Azure Local, while using Azure Arc to manage SQL Server resources through Azure.
  • Azure Local Disconnected Operations (ALDO): Run SQL Server in environments where external connectivity is restricted, intermittent, or unavailable, with operations continuing locally.

This means organizations can choose the deployment approach that fits the requirements of individual environments rather than making the same connectivity decision across their entire data estate.

Bring AI closer to your data

Modernizing infrastructure is only part of the opportunity. Organizations also want to bring generative AI to existing enterprise data, including information that cannot leave their environment.

With Foundry Local, customers can run AI models on Azure Local infrastructure alongside SQL Server, bringing inferencing closer to the data. This enables organizations to explore AI-powered applications while keeping sensitive information and processing within their environment.

This can be particularly valuable in sovereign, regulated, and edge scenarios, where organizations want the benefits of AI but need greater control over where models execute and where their data is processed.

The goal is simple: customers should not have to move sensitive data somewhere else simply to begin building intelligent applications around it.

Build on your existing SQL server investments

Modernization should also make it easier to build on existing investments.

SQL Server is licensed separately from the Azure Local infrastructure platform. For connected deployments, customers can use eligible existing SQL Server licenses, including licenses with Software Assurance or qualifying subscriptions, or use pay-as-you-go licensing through Azure Arc.

For fully disconnected deployments, customers can use eligible existing SQL Server licenses through Azure Hybrid Benefit.

This gives organizations options to modernize their SQL Server environments while taking advantage of eligible licensing investments they already own.

A foundation for sovereign and edge data

Enterprise data estates increasingly span cloud, datacenter, edge, and sovereign environments. The opportunity is not to force every workload into the same deployment model, but to give organizations a consistent path to modernization across them.

SQL Server on Azure Local extends that choice to mission-critical SQL Server workloads, helping customers modernize close to their data, applications, and operations while bringing Azure-consistent infrastructure and local AI capabilities into those environments.

SQL Server on Azure Local FAQ

What is SQL Server on Azure Local?

SQL Server on Azure Local lets organizations run SQL Server on Azure Local infrastructure in their own datacenters and edge locations. It supports SQL Server workloads on virtual machines running Windows Server or Linux.

What is the difference between connected and disconnected deployments?

Connected deployments use Azure connectivity and can use Azure Arc to manage SQL Server resources through Azure. Disconnected operations are designed for environments where external connectivity is restricted, intermittent, or unavailable, with operations continuing locally.

Who should consider SQL Server on Azure Local?

It is designed for organizations that need local control because of sovereignty, regulatory, latency, operational continuity, or edge requirements, including public sector, defense, financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, energy, and other regulated or connectivity-constrained environments.

Can customers use existing SQL Server licenses?

Eligible existing SQL Server licenses can be used according to applicable licensing terms. For connected deployments, customers can also use pay-as-you-go licensing through Azure Arc. Fully disconnected deployments use eligible existing licenses through Azure Hybrid Benefit.

Can organizations run AI close to their SQL Server data?

Foundry Local on Azure Local brings AI inference to Azure Local environments and is designed to keep data processing on-premises. As of September 29, 2026, Foundry Local on Azure Local is currently available in preview, so availability and capabilities may change before general availability.

Where can I find deployment guidance?

Microsoft Learn provides guidance for deploying SQL Server on Azure Local, including hardware selection, SQL Server installation, monitoring, performance tuning, high availability, and related Azure hybrid services.

Get Started with SQL Server on Azure Local

SQL Server on Azure Local is generally available for connected and disconnected deployment scenarios.

  • SQL Server on Azure Local – Overview
  • Deploy SQL Server on Azure Local
  • Deploy SQL Server on Azure Local Disconnected Mode
  • Learn more about Azure Arc-enabled SQL Server

entries.title: FabCon and SQLCon 2026 in Barcelona: Building the data foundation for Microsoft Copilot and agents
entries.summary: Microsoft Fabric and SQL innovations announced at FabCon and SQLCon Barcelona 2026 help organizations build trusted data foundations for AI. The post FabCon and SQLCon 2026 in Barcelona: Building the data foundation for Microsoft Copilot and agents appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
One of the defining strengths of the Fabric and SQL communities is how openly people share what they are building and learning. This week, nearly 5,000 data professionals are coming together in Barcelona to do exactly that. Across more than 130 sessions, more than 10 tutorials, community meetups, and roundtable discussions, attendees will exchange practical insights and real-world experiences that others can apply in their own organizations.

The excitement in Barcelona mirrors the momentum we’re seeing throughout Microsoft’s data portfolio. Microsoft Fabric now supports more than 40,000 customers worldwide, and for decades Microsoft SQL Server has provided the backbone of enterprise workloads including more than 90% of the Fortune 500. Customers like Levi Strauss, H&M, and Thomson Reuters are using these capabilities to unify their data estates, ground AI in their business context, and scale while remaining governed and secure.

Today, we’re announcing new innovations across Microsoft Fabric and our database portfolio designed to help organizations power their Frontier Transformation, including deep integrations with the new Microsoft Copilot, agentic app development in Microsoft Power BI, end-to-end observability in Fabric, the database hub, and more.

Enabling Frontier Transformation with Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft Fabric

Software development has changed dramatically. AI is no longer simply helping developers write code faster. Agents are beginning to work across the full development lifecycle, from planning and coding to testing and deployment.

The opportunity now is to bring that same transformation to the rest of the enterprise. But organizations need more than models and agents. They need trusted context: governed data, shared business definitions, operational knowledge, and the guardrails that help AI act reliably.

This is the foundation of Frontier Transformation: embedding AI into core business processes, grounded in an organization’s unique data, knowledge, and workflows. Microsoft is helping enable this transformation through Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft IQ, which connect AI to an organization’s knowledge, data, applications, and business context.

At the center of this system is Fabric IQ, a shared intelligence layer that connects enterprise data, business metrics, and operational context across the Microsoft ecosystem. By combining unified data from Microsoft OneLake, trusted metrics from Power BI semantic models, and operational context from ontologies and real-time intelligence, Fabric IQ gives people and agents a shared understanding of the business.

Powering the new Microsoft Copilot with trusted data from Fabric IQ

Millions of Microsoft 365 users rely on Microsoft Copilot every day to find information, create content, analyze data, and take action in the flow of work. With the introduction of the new Copilot last week, it’s evolving from a conversational assistant into a unified experience where people can assist, delegate, and even build. Home brings Chat and Cowork together, while Code now gives everyone ways to build their own solutions. As Copilot takes on increasingly sophisticated work, access to trusted business context becomes essential.

Today, we are excited to share we are bringing business context from Fabric IQ into Microsoft Copilot, grounding your work in a shared understanding of the business. Microsoft Copilot customers can now tap into AI-powered insights from Fabric as part of their Copilot experience, without additional AI token costs. Fabric IQ in Copilot Chat and Cowork is generally available today, with integration into the new Code experience coming soon through the Frontier program.

For Power BI customers, this semantic foundation is already in place. Business definitions, key metrics, and organizational knowledge captured in trusted Power BI semantic models and reports can now directly inform decisions and actions in Microsoft Copilot. This allows Copilot users to ask business questions and receive AI-powered insights grounded in the semantic data layer their organization already trusts.

As Bogdan Crivat highlights in his Bringing governed analytics into the flow of work: Fabric Analytics at FabCon Europe 2026 blog, this is a key step toward conversational analytics that connects enterprise data, business context, and AI to help people make better decisions.

Check out the following demo to see this in action:

The next evolution of Power BI: Agentic app creation

With more than 425,000 customers across every country and industry, Power BI has helped millions of users turn their data into insights. Today, we are excited to announce the next evolution of Power BI: bringing agentic app creation to Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

Business intelligence has traditionally followed a familiar pattern: analysts modeled data, built reports, and published dashboards for others to consume. Copilot in Power BI has made this process more conversational, helping users explore data and create and refine reports using natural language. Now, AI is enabling users to go beyond uncovering insights to build tools, workflows, and applications directly from their data.

The new agentic app creation experience in Power BI Desktop takes this a step further. Starting with a trusted semantic model, users can describe the application they need, generate it using natural language, preview and edit it in real time, and publish it to Microsoft Fabric without starting from a blank canvas.

While Copilot in Power BI helps you analyze data and build reports, this new experience enables you to create purpose-built data applications. These applications can accept inputs, write back data, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows.

This experience uses our new Fabric Apps capabilities to provide each application with a SQL database in Fabric, authentication, and security. As an application grows, users can expand its functionality and hand it off to developers and IT teams without rebuilding it.

Watch the following demo to see the new experience in action:

Importantly, this experience isn’t limited to Microsoft Fabric capacity customers. Apps in Power BI will be available in preview in the coming weeks to Power BI Pro and Power BI Premium Per User customers as well as Microsoft Fabric capacity customers. This means Power BI Pro and Premium Per User customers, at no additional cost, will also have access to Fabric Apps and Fabric Database capabilities—up to 1 GB per app—along with enterprise-grade security and scale for hosting. Fabric customers can then extend these apps with other Fabric workloads, creating richer applications on their existing data and services.

To learn more about this feature and other innovations coming to Power BI, read Mohammad Ali’s blog, Power BI’s next chapter: The evolution of business intelligence.

Move from idea to production faster with Fabric Apps

AI can accelerate prototyping, but moving an application into production still requires teams to connect data, add business logic, manage infrastructure, and enforce governance. Fabric Apps closes this gap by giving developers a governed application layer on Microsoft Fabric.

Since the initial launch in June 2026, thousands of developers have used Fabric Apps to build AI-powered business applications, operational workflows, and custom experiences on governed data. Using the open-source Rayfin SDK and CLI, developers and coding agents can build application backends and deploy them to Fabric as Fabric Apps.

With the latest enhancements, developers can connect apps directly to Fabric warehouses, SQL databases, lakehouses, and Power BI semantic models without duplicating data, while preserving existing permissions and trusted business logic. New TypeScript backend functions, Secret Store, PostgreSQL support, private-by-default access, and built-in usage and performance metrics provide the services needed to take those apps into production.

Together, these capabilities give developers a faster path from idea to secure, governed, production-ready Fabric Apps while spending less time assembling infrastructure and more time building differentiated application experiences.

Check out what you can build with Rayfin:

Learn more about Rayfin by reading Sachin Patney’s blog, From prompt to production: What’s new in Fabric Apps.

Building an AI-ready data foundation with Microsoft Fabric

While Fabric IQ brings business context into Copilot, applications, and agents, that intelligence should first be created and maintained. Organizations need a foundation that can unify data across sources, transform and prepare it for analysis, and capture business meaning through semantic models and ontologies. Today’s Microsoft Fabric innovations make it easier to build this foundation from end to end.

Unify your data estate with Microsoft OneLake

As organizations scale AI, connecting data is no longer enough. Copilots and agents also need business context, including terminology, relationships, instructions, and domain knowledge, to deliver relevant answers and take informed action. Microsoft OneLake provides an open foundation for connecting data across clouds, applications, and platforms through mirroring and shortcuts.

Share governed data and context with IQ sharing

Today, we’re taking the next step with IQ sharing, now in preview. IQ sharing helps organizations securely share governed data and business context across teams, customers, partners, and ecosystems, making intelligence reusable beyond organizational boundaries. At launch, IQ sharing supports governed tables and files alongside Markdown agent instructions and RDF ontologies, with native support for Fabric IQ ontologies and Power BI semantic models on the roadmap.

EY, S&P Global, TomTom, Financial Fabric, and xMentium are already building integrations with IQ sharing. For example, TomTom is bringing its geospatial and transportation intelligence into Fabric, with available data products discoverable through the OneLake catalog.

Together, mirroring, shortcuts, and IQ sharing create an open data network that enables organizations to connect, access, and collaborate on governed data across teams, partners, and ecosystems. This extends OneLake beyond data integration to support reusable data products that power analytics and AI.

Expanding the OneLake ecosystem

We’re also expanding the reach of that open data network with the preview of bidirectional integration with Salesforce Data Cloud 360, the general availability of Google BigQuery mirroring, and deeper integration with Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central. Now, Salesforce data becomes part of the unified data estate without moving or duplicating it, making it available across Fabric for analytics and AI, including as business context for Fabric data agents.

Additionally, we are rapidly growing the OneLake ecosystem with Atlan, dbt, and ClickHouse, making it easier to bring trusted business context to OneLake data, transform it using familiar developer workflows, and work with it from external analytical engines.

Together, these capabilities make it easier to work across platforms, tools, and clouds without duplicating data or building complex integrations. Learn more about all the innovation coming to Microsoft OneLake by reading Dipti Borkar’s blog, FabCon and SQLCon Barcelona 2026: What’s new in Microsoft OneLake and its rapidly growing ecosystem.

Process and harmonize data more efficiently

Connecting data is only the first step. Organizations still need to prepare, transform, and operationalize data at scale. To help teams move faster from data to insight and action, we’re introducing data engineering agent in Microsoft Fabric, and new Copilot experiences in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence.

Delegate complex data engineering work to data engineering agents

As AI becomes part of the development process, data engineers are evolving from executing every task themselves to orchestrating intelligent systems. Fabric is taking the next step in that evolution with the data engineering agent, built on technology from Microsoft’s acquisition of Osmos earlier this year. Now in preview, the data engineering agent brings governed, autonomous execution to complex, long-running initiatives such as data platform migrations, lakehouse modernization, performance optimization, complex extracting, transforming, and loading (ETL), and data preparation.

Engineers define the desired outcome and establish guardrails. Within those boundaries, the agents then plan and execute the work autonomously, validate results and refine its approach, helping teams move complex data initiatives forward while keeping engineers in control.

Fabric data engineering agent is also designed for collaborative work that spans people and teams. Tasks inherit workspace permissions, enabling authorized team members to monitor progress, contribute context, respond to decisions, and work together on the same task.

And because data engineers work across multiple development environments, these capabilities extend across Fabric and developer tools, including GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Codex, and Claude Code. Engineers can start, monitor, and steer the same work from the tools they already use without losing context or progress.

Learn more about the Fabric data engineering agent in Bogdan Crivat’s blog, Bringing governed analytics into the flow of work: Fabric Analytics at FabCon Europe 2026.

Simplify working with real-time data with Copilot

Organizations increasingly need to act on live operational signals, not just historical reports. New Copilot capabilities in Real-Time Intelligence help teams understand, monitor, and manage real-time data using natural language. Users can now create Real-Time Dashboards by describing what they want to understand, while Copilot assists users with eventhouse management and administrative tasks such as creating tables, configuring policies, managing schema, and inspecting cluster state.

New schema recommendations and optimization capabilities further help organizations improve performance and reduce costs, while the operations agent accelerates troubleshooting with AI-powered root cause analysis and actionable recommendations. Learn more about Real-Time Intelligence innovations in Yitzhak Kesselman’s blog, Trusted AI starts with Microsoft Fabric, Real-Time Intelligence, and IQ.

Curate context with Fabric IQ

With data unified and prepared, organizations need a way to capture the business meaning, relationships, rules, and operational context that AI depends on. Fabric IQ provides this shared intelligence layer, extending governed business context across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, GitHub Copilot, and custom applications to help agents reason over a common understanding of the business.

Accelerate ontology creation and governance

Today, we are making it easier to define and govern this context layer. We are introducing a new agentic experience to create ontologies from semantic models, OneLake data, and other context documents, reducing the effort required to capture business concepts and relationships.

You can define rules in natural language, connect them to ontology entities, properties, and relationships, and make them part of the shared context people and agents use to navigate business operations consistently. You can also carry Power BI measures into your ontology, allowing you to reuse these established metrics.

We’re also affirming our commitment to Apache Ossie (incubating), a community-led effort to establish a vendor-neutral standard for exchanging semantic metadata across analytics, AI, and BI platforms. Working with Snowflake and the broader industry, we’re helping make semantic context open and reusable across platforms.

Together, these capabilities make it easier to maintain shared business meaning and help agents reason over governed data with greater accuracy and consistency. Learn more about Fabric IQ in Yitzhak Kesselman’s blog, Trusted AI starts with Microsoft Fabric, Real-Time Intelligence, and IQ.

Create and manage agents in Fabric

The value of a shared intelligence foundation comes when agents can use that context to deliver real outcomes. New enhancements across Fabric agents make it easier to build, govern, and operationalize AI experiences across Microsoft Fabric and other AI platforms.

We are deepening the integration between Fabric data agents and ontologies in Fabric IQ, enabling more accurate and explainable answers grounded in business concepts and relationships. The build agent with AI mode can now use semantic models, documentation, glossaries, and data dictionaries to generate richer data agent experiences with less manual configuration. Operations agents are adding pre-approved actions and new root-cause analysis into preview, helping teams investigate issues, identify likely causes, and automate repeatable responses while maintaining human oversight and control. Learn more about these updates by visiting Bogdan Crivat’s blog, Bringing governed analytics into the flow of work: Fabric Analytics at FabCon Europe 2026, and Yitzhak Kesselman’s blog, Trusted AI starts with Microsoft Fabric, Real-Time Intelligence, and IQ.

Operate Fabric with greater visibility and control

As organizations place more workloads on a unified data platform, operational maturity becomes as important as analytical capability. Teams need to understand what is happening across jobs, capacities, workspaces, and services—and resolve issues before they affect the business.

Introducing new observability capabilities in Microsoft Fabric

Observability in Fabric, now in preview, is a new set of platform capabilities designed to help organizations move from reactive troubleshooting to proactive operations. Spanning workspace monitoring, the monitor hub, and operations agents, these new observability capabilities provide a unified view of the Fabric estate, making it easier to detect issues early, investigate root causes with AI assistance, and manage operations from a single experience.

The new workspace monitoring experience allows you to consolidate telemetry in a single eventhouse for multiple workspaces, simplifying cross-workspace monitoring. You can even make the data available in other destinations with custom endpoints and control the exact retention rate and caching policy you need.

We’ve also enhanced the monitor hub in Fabric with deeper visibility into jobs, capacities, and workloads through built-in views, alerts, and AI-powered insights. New Activator-powered job alerts notify teams of job failures and successes, while a new capacity view helps monitor consumption and headroom. In addition, we’ve added new investigation capabilities to operations agents, helping data professionals and administrators diagnose issues faster by autonomously identifying root causes and recommended actions.

Together, these capabilities reduce the effort required to identify problems, improve reliability, and keep data and AI workloads running smoothly.

Check out the demo below to see observability in action:

Pay only for what you consume with on-demand billing

Visibility is only part of the equation. Organizations also need flexible, predictable ways to align infrastructure costs with usage as data and AI workloads scale.

Building on Autoscale Billing for Spark, on-demand billing expands consumption-based billing across Fabric workloads, allowing you to pay only for the compute you use, automatically scaling resources up and down based on your demand. Fabric zero-provisioned adds to on-demand billing by allowing you to get started with Fabric and OneLake without an upfront capacity commitment.

To learn more about observability in Fabric, on-demand billing, and other innovation coming to the Fabric platform, read Kim Manis’s blog, Build, deploy, and govern Microsoft Fabric at scale.

Manage, optimize, and scale your database estate

Building intelligent applications requires more than powerful AI models. Organizations also need databases that can scale with demand, tools to manage growing data estates, and intelligent operations that keep systems running reliably.

Today, we’re introducing new capabilities across Database Hub, Database Agents, and Microsoft Azure SQL Database that help organizations build, manage, and optimize the data foundation behind the next generation of intelligent applications.

Centrally manage your database estate with the Database Hub in Fabric and database agents

As developers build more applications and operational workloads move into Fabric, managing a growing database estate becomes just as important as building applications. Organizations need a unified way to monitor, govern, and optimize these databases.

Building on its introduction at FabCon & SQLCon Atlanta, Database Hub in Fabric is now in preview. It provides a centralized control plane for managing SQL Server, Microsoft Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, Azure Cosmos DB, and SQL database in Fabric. From a single experience, administrators can monitor health, assess risk, enforce governance, and gain visibility across their entire database estate.

Additionally, we are introducing database agents for SQL and PostgreSQL on Azure, which will soon be available in preview. These AI-powered specialist agents, accessible in the Database Hub in Fabric and VS Code, continuously observe and analyze database signals, helping administrators investigate issues, understand performance bottlenecks, identify optimization opportunities, and accelerate troubleshooting. By bringing AI-assisted operations directly into a unified management experience, teams can move from insights to action faster while improving reliability, performance, and security.

Together, these innovations provide the operational foundation for intelligent applications across Microsoft, helping organizations manage their data estate with the same simplicity, scale, and intelligence that powers analytics and AI in Microsoft Fabric.

Learn more about the Database Hub and database agents in Shireesh Thota’s blog, SQLCon Barcelona 2026: Advancing SQL with greater control, scale, and intelligence.

Bringing greater scale, efficiency, and AI innovation to Azure SQL Database Hyperscale

Intelligent applications place new demands on databases, requiring greater scale, efficiency, and built-in support for AI-powered scenarios. We’re introducing new innovations in Azure SQL Database Hyperscale designed to help developers reduce costs, scale demanding applications, and build AI-powered experiences using familiar SQL tools.

Serverless auto-pause for Azure SQL Database Hyperscale, now in preview, automatically pauses compute during periods of inactivity and resumes when workloads return, helping reduce costs for development, test, and intermittent workloads. We’re also increasing elastic pool density to support up to 50 databases per pool and making 192 vCore compute for Azure SQL Database Hyperscale generally available, enabling greater scale and concurrency for mission-critical applications.

In addition, we’re announcing the general availability of DiskANN vector indexes for Azure SQL Database Hyperscale, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and SQL database in Fabric, bringing high-performance vector search directly into the database engine. Developers can build recommendation engines, semantic search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications without moving data to a separate vector store.

Enable sovereign data across customer-controlled environments

Organizations need the flexibility to run data platforms where performance, regulatory, and operational requirements demand. Microsoft is expanding where customers can run Azure and SQL Server capabilities, enabling modern workloads across sovereign, customer-controlled data estates—whether on the cloud, edge, or in disconnected environments.

SQL Server on Azure Local is now generally available, bringing SQL Server and Azure capabilities to local environments. Organizations can run mission-critical workloads closer to their applications and operations for low-latency, high-performance access to data while maintaining control over where data resides. In addition, SQL Server on Azure Local Disconnected Operations (ALDO) is also now generally available, enabling the same platform and experience in environments where cloud connectivity is unavailable, restricted, or intentionally disconnected.

Whether supporting regulated industries, operating at the edge, or running business-critical systems in disconnected environments, customers can now bring modern Azure and database capabilities closer to their data while maintaining the performance, control, and flexibility their workloads require.

Finally, Microsoft Fabric is expanding to Microsoft 365 Government Community Cloud High (GCC High) customers, supporting organizations that require United States sovereign cloud environments and compliance.

Learn more about all the innovation we are bringing to our database offerings by reading Shireesh Thota’s blog, SQLCon Barcelona 2026: Advancing SQL with greater control, scale, and intelligence.

Discover more Fabric and Azure Database innovation

AI transformation will not be defined by how many agents organizations create, but by how effectively those agents understand the business and work together to deliver outcomes. The organizations that build a trusted, connected data foundation now will be best positioned to lead.

For a deeper look at the updates above and to see what else is new this month, visit the Fabric September 2026 Feature Summary blog, the Power BI September 2026 Feature Summary blog, and the latest posts on the Fabric Updates channel and the Azure Data Tech Community blog channel.

entries.title: Enhancing Microsoft Azure Virtual Machine lifecycle
entries.summary: Our Virtual Machine Lifecycle policy guides how we manage these transitions, giving Azure customers transparency, predictability, and guidance. The post Enhancing Microsoft Azure Virtual Machine lifecycle appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
Azure continuously advances through new infrastructure generations, platform capabilities, services, and innovations that lead the industry in performance, security, reliability, and efficiency. Our Virtual Machine (VM) Lifecycle policy guides how we manage these transitions, giving Azure customers transparency, predictability, and guidance to plan for and execute technology changes with confidence. Our goal is to help every organization plan and navigate these modernization steps in line with Azure’s latest innovations and ongoing platform investments.

To give you access to the most advanced cloud and AI infrastructure, deployed on the most sophisticated silicon and hardware, the Azure Virtual Machine lifecycle is built around three customer outcomes:

  • Transparency to easily understand the lifecycle status of Azure technologies, Microsoft’s level of ongoing investment, and the recommended path forward as new innovations become available.
  • Predictability to plan against defined lifecycle stages, understand what to expect at each stage, and advance notice as technologies progress through their lifecycle.
  • Guidance to help you modernize and adopt newer technologies rapidly and with confidence, along with AI-led tooling to accelerate workload transitions and recommendations.

This lifecycle provides a shared taxonomy, common stages, and consistent commitments for how we communicate technology evolution.

Azure General Purpose, Memory Optimized, Compute Optimized, and Storage Optimized VMs are the first VM families covered by this policy.

The lifecycle stages, spanning Current, Extended, End of Life, and Retired, are defined below, with dedicated Microsoft investment levels, regional and quota availability, applicable purchasing options, and pricing. The policy establishes clear lifecycle stages, expected customer experiences, and Microsoft’s commitments at each stage so customers can confidently plan, deploy, and modernize workloads over time.

Azure Virtual Machine Lifecycle Policy
Stage Description
Current Customer recommendation: Customers can confidently deploy new workloads, expand existing deployments, and optimize their Azure investments using VMs in the Current stage of the lifecycle. These VMs are specifically recommended for new deployments.

Microsoft investment: During this stage, products receive standard maintenance and support.

Availability: Current VM series are generally available to customers and have broad availability across Azure regions globally.

Purchasing options and pricing: Pay-as-you-go pricing and Azure Savings Plans. Azure Reserved VM Instances may also be offered.
Extended Customer recommendation: Azure VMs in the Extended stage remain supported for existing workloads; however, customers should begin evaluating and planning a transition to VMs in the Current stage.

Microsoft investment: During this stage, products continue to receive standard maintenance and support.

Availability: VMs in the Extended stage remain generally available across multiple regions. However, VMs in this stage may be subject to quota restrictions. Purchasing options and pricing: Pay-as-you-go pricing and Azure Savings Plans. Azure Reserved VM Instances may also be offered. Changes to purchasing options and pricing are possible.
End of Life Customer recommendation: VMs enter the End of Life stage when their retirement is formally announced. These VMs are based on older platform generations and do not benefit from the latest advancements in performance, security, reliability, and efficiency. Customers should actively plan and transition the workloads to VMs in the Current or Extended stages.

Microsoft investment: During this stage, products continue to receive standard maintenance and support. In addition, Azure will provide notifications, migration tooling, and guidance to help customers move to newer versions.

Availability: VMs in the End of Life stage remain available to existing customers in currently supported regions and within their existing quota allocations, subject to available capacity. New deployments and quota requests are subject to restriction. Microsoft will deploy new workload placement capabilities for VMs in the End of Life stage. While customers may experience minor workload performance variations in rare scenarios, existing Azure Virtual Machines SLAs will be met. These capabilities allow Microsoft to improve capacity availability for VMs in the End of Life stage as well as help support continued investments in modern hardware, new capabilities, and global scale.

Purchasing options and pricing: Pay-as-you-go pricing and Azure Savings Plans remain available, while Reserved Instances may no longer be offered. When VMs enter the End of Life stage, customers should expect changes to pricing and availability.
Retired Customer recommendation: Retired VMs are no longer available and can no longer be provisioned. Customer modernization should be complete, with workloads now deployed to VMs in the Current or Extended stages.

Microsoft investment: VMs in a Retired series are no longer covered by a service level agreement (SLA) and are not eligible for Microsoft support.

Availability: New VM creation is no longer available, and existing VMs will be deallocated.

Purchasing options and pricing: VMs in a retired series are no longer available for purchase.

Note: Lifecycle details described in this policy represent general guidance and may be subject to product-specific, regional, or operational exceptions.

Platform experiences and tools to help simplify transitions

Microsoft is committed to helping you modernize your workload portfolio with the greatest possible speed, confidence, and simplicity. Azure Advisor and Azure Service Health give you clear insight into your subscriptions and resources—helping you discover upcoming VM retirements, identify affected resources, and track your modernization progress with recommended actions built in. Beyond this, Microsoft is investing in intelligent, AI-augmented tools designed to apply lifecycle guidance across your entire workload portfolio, further reducing friction as you modernize.

Microsoft is committed to helping you navigate these infrastructure transitions and take advantage of the next wave of innovation. As Azure continues to advance, our commitment is to make change predictable, transparent, and supported through clear lifecycle guidance, early visibility, and practical help to modernize with confidence. This policy is an important step toward making modernization easier to plan, simpler to execute, and more valuable for every Azure customer.

For more information about the Azure Virtual Machines lifecycle, visit the VM lifecycle overview page.

Azure Virtual Machines

Create and manage virtual machines
